doc.title: Annie Ross interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001

title: The trio's impact, the Flamingo and getting along
summary: The group changed vocal groups; at the Flamingo in Vegas the mics were turned off because crowds stopped gambling; they had run-ins but loved each other.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Well yeah. No one had done it. I mean it really changed vocal groups, and we spawned many, many — you know, New York Voices. Plus, we were so weird you know. There was Dave, from New England, there was Jon, from Toledo, and there was me, from Scotland, and when we played Vegas at the Flamingo, the second night they turned off all the mics because we were detracting from the gambling. People would hear us and they’d come and they’d stop and they’d look, and the tables were losing ‘em.
Yeah. And the next day, our throats, you know, from trying to project. But we were startling.
Um hum, you sure did. Yeah a lot of people cite this group as a major find.
And you know we worked, we played to the people too. Besides being able to hit the notes, we had three individual personalities.
No? That’s a hard thing — being that close —

You’re bound to have, you know, run-ins. But we did love each other, especially when we worked. I mean it was magic. You could want to kill somebody, and you’d do your thing together and forget about it.
You sound just like a trumpet, it’s unbelievable.
